extracted.subtask_description: Guidance for determining correct inventor(s) to be named in U.S. patent applications where inventions were created by natural persons with assistance from one or more artificial intelligence systems. Instructs examiners on when to raise inventorship questions, when to require information, and how existing statutes/regulations apply.

rubrics_metrics.name: Inventor must be a natural person
rubrics_metrics.description: An inventor or joint inventor in a patent application must be a natural person; non-persons (e.g., AI systems) cannot be named as inventors.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: If an applicant lists a non-person as an inventor (e.g., an AI system), the claims must be rejected by the examiner under 35 U.S.C. § 101 and § 115 since an inventor may only be a natural person. This rule is grounded in the Federal Circuit decision Thaler v. Vidal (43 F.4th 1207 (Fed. Cir. 2022)).

rubrics_metrics.name: AI-assisted inventions are not categorically unpatentable
rubrics_metrics.description: Patent protection may be sought for inventions in which a natural person provided a significant contribution, even if AI systems assisted in creation.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The Federal Circuit's holding that inventors must be natural persons does not address patent eligibility of AI-assisted inventions. The Office's position is that AI-assisted inventions can be patentable where at least one human provided a significant contribution and can be named as an inventor.

rubrics_metrics.name: Apply the significant contribution test for inventorship
rubrics_metrics.description: Use the longstanding 'significant contribution' test (applied since Pannu v. Iolab) to evaluate whether a person contributed sufficiently to be an inventor for AI-assisted inventions.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The Inventorship Guidance provides a framework and examples for applying the significant contribution test to AI-assisted inventions. Examiners should follow that guidance when deciding whether a natural person's contribution rises to inventorship.

rubrics_metrics.name: Presumption in favor of named inventors
rubrics_metrics.description: The Office presumes that the named inventor(s) in an application are the actual inventor(s). Examiners should only raise inventorship questions in rare instances where the file record or extrinsic evidence suggests otherwise.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Because inventorship questions during examination are uncommon, examiners must have satisfactory indication from the record or extrinsic evidence before contesting named inventors. The guidance does not anticipate a significant change in how inventorship is evaluated generally.

rubrics_metrics.name: Rejection/grounds when inventorship appears incorrect
rubrics_metrics.description: Failure to name the correct inventor(s) is a ground of rejection under 35 U.S.C. §§ 101 and 115; examiners must make a rejection when there is sufficient evidence that inventorship is incorrect.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examples include when a non-person is listed as inventor. If the file record or extrinsic evidence calls into question whether the named inventor(s) are proper, the examiner should act (rejection) and consult the Inventorship Guidance and TC POC as needed.

rubrics_metrics.name: Examiners may require further information under 37 CFR 1.105
rubrics_metrics.description: When further information is reasonably necessary to properly examine or treat a matter (including inventorship issues), examiners may require information from the applicant under 37 CFR 1.105.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: In AI-assisted invention cases, this could include information regarding each named inventor's contributions to the claimed invention and how an AI system was used in creating the invention. Before making such a requirement, examiners should consult their Technology Center Point of Contact (TC POC) to ensure consistency with Technology Center policies.

rubrics_metrics.name: Consult Technology Center Point of Contact (TC POC)
rubrics_metrics.description: If the file record or extrinsic evidence relating to an AI-assisted invention calls inventorship into question, the examiner should consult a TC POC on applying the Inventorship Guidance to determine correct inventorship.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Consultation helps ensure consistent application of the guidance across Technology Centers and appropriateness of any requirements for information or rejections. Examiners are specifically instructed to use TC POCs before taking certain actions (e.g., requesting information under 1.105).

rubrics_metrics.name: Inventorship corrections during examination (37 CFR 1.48)
rubrics_metrics.description: Inventorship can generally be corrected during examination under 37 CFR 1.48; OPAP typically processes most requests to correct inventorship.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: A request for correction of inventorship that has been approved may be grounds to withdraw an inventorship rejection under 35 U.S.C. § 101 and § 115 or to withdraw a requirement for information under 37 CFR 1.105. See MPEP § 602.01(c)(1).

rubrics_metrics.name: No new general AI-disclosure requirement
rubrics_metrics.description: The Office is not implementing any new general requirement to disclose the use of AI beyond existing rules; disclosure of AI use is required only where existing rules make it necessary.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Disclosure of AI use may still be required in rare circumstances if material to patentability under Rule 1.56 (duty of disclosure) or reasonably necessary to properly examine or treat a matter under Rule 1.105. Recognizes that as AI becomes ubiquitous it may become harder to identify AI's role, but currently no blanket disclosure rule is added.

rubrics_metrics.name: Follow the Inventorship Guidance over inconsistent MPEP sections
rubrics_metrics.description: To the extent earlier Office guidance or certain MPEP sections are inconsistent with the AI Inventorship Guidance, Office personnel are to follow the AI Inventorship Guidance.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The MPEP will be updated in due course to reflect the new guidance. Examiners should follow the Inventorship Guidance immediately where inconsistency exists.

rubrics_metrics.name: Focus on whether at least one human can be and is listed as inventor
rubrics_metrics.description: In examining AI-assisted inventions, what matters is whether at least one human can be (and is) listed as an inventor; it is irrelevant if AI or advanced computer systems performed actions that might otherwise rise to inventorship.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: From an examiner's perspective, treat actions by AI like actions by other advanced computer systems — the key is the human contribution and that no non-humans are listed as inventors.
